verdict: OK to lend selectively in Noida IT services — pursue mid-size domestic-focused and GCC-support firms with 90-day-or-better receivables; avoid US-concentrated billable-hour shops and sub-scale startups until the AI city moves past in-principle approval.
title: Noida Computer Software & IT: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Noida software firm sells skilled people and code, not inventory — cash turns on the receivable cycle, not on stock.** Revenue is billed monthly against contracts; the cost base is salaries, bench time, subcontractor fees and office rent, with almost no raw material. Pricing power sits with firms that own a product or a sticky managed-service contract; pure staff-augmentation shops price at the client's rate card. **So when a proposal lands, check the contract mix first: fixed-price and managed-service work earns margin, time-and-material work earns only utilisation.**

## What has changed now
**The local news is a land and policy signal, not yet a revenue signal.** Noida Authority has given in-principle approval to an AI city-cum-business park with at least 50 per cent of built-up area reserved for IT and knowledge-based services [1], aimed at GCCs, IT firms and start-ups [2], under the UP Private Business Park Development Scheme, 2025, with bids still to be invited for a master developer [3]. **Nothing here is built or leased yet — treat it as a 2027-plus pipeline, not 2026 cash flow.** Peer results are mixed: InfoBeans grew 22 per cent in constant currency but profit growth of 16 per cent trailed revenue of 30 per cent, with rising 90-day receivables [4]; TCS held margins while its stock is down 30.3 per cent year-to-date as AI undermines billable-hour work [5]; Cognizant's Q3 beat lifted the Nifty IT index nearly 2 per cent [6]; Sasken grew revenue 25.6 per cent to Rs 321 crores with EBITDA margin up 700 basis points [7]. **Read together: growth is real for focused mid-caps, but the billable-hour model is being repriced.** Rating methodology notes (undated, treat as background) flag US revenue concentration and visa norms as structural risks [9]. **Take monthly: receivable ageing by client, billed-versus-collected, employee count and attrition, and top-five client concentration.** Structure as a working-capital line sized to the receivable cycle, not a term loan for office fit-out; take a charge on receivables and a personal guarantee. **If receivables cross 90 days, ask for the client name and contract; if one client exceeds 30 per cent of revenue, cap exposure.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch unbilled revenue rising faster than billed revenue — that is work done but not accepted, and it is the first place a software lender loses money.** Watch bench strength and salary delays; watch a shift from fixed-price to time-and-material without a margin explanation. **Sources say little about Noida-specific borrower data, so lean on these first-principles checks plus the peer numbers above.**

Headcount falls over 10% in a quarter -> re-underwrite contract pipeline
